To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) Phrase-based MT (PBMT) and Neural MT (NMT) models perform equally well for AMR-to- text generation.

(1) the Neural MT model outperforms the Phrase-based MT model, (2) the Delexicalisation step helps both MT models, (3) the Compression step helps the Phrase-based MT and (4) the Linearisation step helps both models.

(1) Delexicalization, compression and linearization are beneficial preprocessing techniques; (2) Neural MT outperforms Phrase-based MT; (3) The combination of preprocessing techniques and Neural MT achieves the best results; (4) The combination of Neural MT and compression achieves a significant improvement over the best results reported in the literature.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the generation of text from AMR graphs.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
AMR-to-text translation is still an open problem and that more research is needed.

(1) the best performing AMR-to-text model is a combination of phrase-based MT with delexicalisation, compression and linearisation; (2) the second best model is a combination phrase-based MT with only compression and linearisation (3) the third best model is a neural MT model with compression and linearisation.
• The Neural MT model outperforms the Phrasebased model in terms of BLEU and ROUGE, but the difference in ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-2 is not significant.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
AMR-to-text can be viewed as a translation task, where the AMR preprocessing steps are beneficial.
AMR is a very interesting representation for translation.
AMR-to-text translation is a challenging problem and that the choice of the MT model is an important factor.
The main takeaway from our work is that

AMR-to-text is a challenging task and the best approach depends on the MT model used.
